blocks.text: OOP has core concepts that make programs organised, reusable and easier to manage: classes and objects, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
Classes and objects: representing real-world entities

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: A class is like a blueprint, while an object is the real thing created from that blueprint.

A class is a blueprint or template that defines the properties (attributes) and actions (methods) of an entity. An object is an instance of a class that holds actual values for its attributes (Fig 3.1). Classes and objects let programmers model real-world entities and keep data and its related functions together, which makes programs more structured.

blocks.alt: Class and object diagram: a box Class: Person lists Attributes (name, age, gender) and Methods (eat(), sleep(), work()) beside a person silhouette. Arrows lead to Object P1 (name = Bob, age = 34, gender = Male; eat(), sleep(), work()) with a picture of a man, and Object P2 (name = Jenny, age = 27, gender = Female; eat(), sleep(), work()) with a picture of a woman.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.1: Diagram Showing Class and Object relationship (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.1).

blocks.title: Example: a Student class (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
class Student:
....def __init__(self, name):
........self.name = name

....def display(self):
........print("Student Name:", self.name)

# Creating objects
object1 = Student("Ali")
object2 = Student("Ahmed")

# Using objects
object1.display()
object2.display()

items: class Student defines a blueprint for students.
__init__ sets the name when an object is created.
object1 and object2 are two different Student objects, each with its own data (Ali, Ahmed).

blocks.text: Encapsulation

blocks.title: Encapsulation
blocks.text: Encapsulation means bundling data (variables) and methods (functions) into a single unit, the class, and restricting direct access to the data.

Unlike Java or C++, Python has no strict 'private' or 'protected' keywords; it uses naming conventions to signal how data should be accessed. Encapsulation protects data from unwanted access, improves security, makes code easier to manage and allows only controlled changes. Think of a bank account: your balance is hidden, you can reach it only through deposit() and withdraw(), and you cannot change it directly.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Hide the data and control access using methods.

blocks.caption: Levels of access control in Python
rows: Accessible from anywhere, inside or outside the class; all members are public by default
Meant for use inside the class and its subclasses; a convention, not enforced
Hard to reach from outside: Python's name mangling changes the internal name to prevent accidental access

blocks.alt: Encapsulation diagram: a User / Outside Class box. A green arrow with a tick, labelled Access allowed, goes to the Public Methods / Interface box (getValue(), setValue()) inside a Class Object box; a dotted arrow leads from the methods to the Private Data box (__private_variable). A red dashed line with a cross, labelled Direct access restricted, runs from the user to the private data.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.2: Encapsulation diagram showing private and public variables (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 3.2 labels the private data _private_variable with one underscore, which in Python marks a protected member; a private member has two underscores, __private_variable, as drawn above.

blocks.title: Example: encapsulation in a BankAccount (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
class BankAccount:
....def __init__(self, balance):
........self.__balance = balance      # private variable

....def deposit(self, amount):
........self.__balance += amount

....def withdraw(self, amount):
........if amount <= self.__balance:
............self.__balance -= amount
........else:
............print("Insufficient balance")

....def get_balance(self):
........return self.__balance

# Usage
account = BankAccount(1000)
account.deposit(500)
account.withdraw(300)
print(account.get_balance())      # Output: 1200

# Direct access will fail
# print(account.__balance)        # Error
Inheritance: reusing and extending functionality

Inheritance lets a class take the properties and methods of another class. The new class, called a subclass or child class, can add to or modify the features of the parent class (superclass). Inheritance promotes code reuse, reduces redundancy and makes it easier to extend a program without rewriting existing code. A child class is defined by writing the parent's name in brackets: class Child(Parent):.

items: Single inheritance: a child class inherits from exactly one parent class (Fig 3.3). It is the most basic form.

blocks.alt: Single inheritance: a Child Class box below a Parent Class box, joined by a line with a hollow arrowhead at the Parent Class.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.3: Single Inheritance (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.3).

blocks.title: Example: single inheritance (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
# Parent class (superclass)
class Animal:
....def __init__(self, name):
........self.name = name

....def eat(self):
........print(f"{self.name} is eating.")

# Child class (subclass) inheriting from Animal
class Dog(Animal):
....def bark(self):
........print(f"{self.name} says Woof!")

my_dog = Dog("Buddy")
my_dog.eat()     # Output: Buddy is eating.
my_dog.bark()    # Output: Buddy says Woof!

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: self is the reference to the current object; Python passes it automatically to instance methods.

items: Parent class (base class): the class whose properties are inherited; Animal above.
Child class (derived class): the class that inherits; Dog above.
Method overriding: a child class can give its own version of a method its parent already has. Inside it, super() calls the parent's version.
Multiple inheritance: a child class inherits from more than one parent class and combines their behaviour, for example a Smartphone class inheriting from both Camera and Computer (Fig 3.4).

blocks.alt: Multiple inheritance: a Child Class box below two boxes, Parent Class 1 and Parent Class 2; lines from the child go to both parents, each ending in a hollow arrowhead at the parent.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.4: Multiple Inheritance (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.4).

blocks.title: Example: multiple inheritance (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
class Father:
....def skill1(self):
........print("Father's skill: Gardening")

class Mother:
....def skill2(self):
........print("Mother's skill: Cooking")

# Derived class inheriting from two base classes
class Child(Father, Mother):
....def own_skill(self):
........print("Child's skill: Coding")

c = Child()
c.skill1()      # Father's method
c.skill2()      # Mother's method
c.own_skill()   # its own method

items: Multilevel inheritance: a class inherits from a class that is itself derived, forming a chain like a family tree (grandparent, parent, child); the 'grandchild' gets the methods and attributes of both its parent and its grandparent (Fig 3.5).

blocks.alt: Multilevel inheritance: three boxes in a column, Grand Parent Class at the top, Parent Class in the middle and Child Class at the bottom; each lower class is joined to the one above by a line with a hollow arrowhead at the upper class.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.5: Multilevel Inheritance (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.5).

blocks.title: Example: multilevel inheritance (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
# Base class (grandparent)
class Vehicle:
....def start_engine(self):
........print("Engine started.")

# Intermediate class (parent)
class Car(Vehicle):
....def drive(self):
........print("Car is driving.")

# Derived class (child)
class ElectricCar(Car):
....def charge(self):
........print("Battery is charging.")

my_tesla = ElectricCar()
my_tesla.start_engine()   # inherited from Vehicle
my_tesla.drive()          # inherited from Car
my_tesla.charge()         # defined in ElectricCar

blocks.title: Class activity
blocks.text: Create a Vehicle class and extend it with Car and Bike subclasses. Add a unique method to each subclass and demonstrate inheritance.
Polymorphism

Polymorphism means 'many forms'. The same method, function or operator can behave differently depending on the object it works with, which makes code more flexible and reusable. For example, a payment system may offer credit card, UPI, net banking and wallet payments. All of them use a common method, processPayment(), but each has its own implementation; net banking, for instance, redirects the user to the bank's login page. The method name stays the same while the action changes with the payment type.
There are two main types of polymorphism, compile-time and runtime (Fig 3.6).

blocks.alt: Polymorphism tree: Polymorphism branches into Compile-time Polymorphism, which leads to Method Overloading, and Runtime Polymorphism, which leads to Method Overriding.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.6: Polymorphism example showing the same function behaving differently (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.6).

items: Compile-time polymorphism: the method to run is chosen during compilation, usually through method or operator overloading, as in Java or C++. Python does not support true overloading by function signature: because it is dynamically typed, one function can accept arguments of different types. Similar behaviour is achieved with default arguments, variable-length arguments (*args, **kwargs) or conditions inside the function.

Runtime polymorphism (overriding): the behaviour is decided while the program runs, according to the object calling the method. It happens through method overriding, when a child class provides its own version of a method already defined in the parent.

blocks.title: Example: overloading imitated with default and variable-length arguments (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
class Calculator:
....def multiply(self, a=1, b=1, *args):
........result = a * b
........for num in args:
............result *= num
........return result

calc = Calculator()
print(calc.multiply())          # 1   (default arguments)
print(calc.multiply(4))         # 4
print(calc.multiply(2, 3))      # 6   (more arguments)
print(calc.multiply(2, 3, 4))   # 24

blocks.title: Example: runtime polymorphism by overriding (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)

blocks.text: The same call, animal.sound(), gives a different result for a Dog, a Cat or a plain Animal, and the choice is made at runtime. This dynamic behaviour makes Python well suited to runtime polymorphism.
